Lessons.Title: Area and the Multiplication Table (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Explore how the area of a rectangle helps us organize multiplication facts. This optional lesson deepens the connection between area and multiplication; the factors along the top and left edge of a multiplication table label side lengths, and the cell where they meet contains their product. Header cells are labels, not square units in the rectangle.

Warm-up — Arrays that Grow: look at each dot arrangement, think quietly, then tell a partner how many dots you see and how you see them. The first picture has two rows of four. In the second, a two-by-two block joins the first array. In the third, a further two-by-two block joins it. Decompose the pictures into smaller arrays or groups of four. Compare different decompositions; explain why each dot is counted once. Restate a partner’s strategy before adding your own observation.

Area and the Multiplication Table: inspect the four five-by-five tables in the companion. Each rectangle begins at the upper-left DATA square, just below and to the right of the headers. Three rows and one, two, three or four columns give products 3, 6, 9 and 12 in the lower-right corner of the rectangle. The changing factor adds one column of three squares each time. Share a notice and a question; record these so everyone can refer to them.

First create your own rectangle in a blank five-by-five table. Start at the upper-left data square, trace its bottom and right boundaries, and write the product in its lower-right square. Read its two factors from the headers. Count its squares to check the multiplication and explain your drawing to a partner. Different rectangles are allowed; a teacher checks the actual drawing.

Next use the nine-by-nine table to create a rectangle of area 24 square units. All its sides must fit in the table. A three-by-eight rectangle and a four-by-six rectangle both work; rotating either also works. A two-by-twelve rectangle has area 24 but does not fit this table. Start in the upper-left data square and record 24 in the lower-right square of the rectangle. Share and compare several solutions rather than treating one pair of factors as the only answer.

Products in the Multiplication Table: inspect the ten-by-ten table, initially containing only some products in the row and column for 2. Write a notice and a question. Independently find as many other products as you can; start with familiar rows and columns for 2, 5 and 10. Completing every cell is not required. Discuss how a known fact helps you find a nearby unfamiliar fact.

With your class, finish the row and column for 2 and those for 5. In the row for 5, the products increase by 5 when the column factor increases by 1. The ones digits alternate 5 and 0. Matching positions in the row and column for 5 have the same product: 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 3 = 15. Think quietly, discuss with a partner, and write your own equations for a pattern you notice. Rehearse your explanation with a partner before sharing it with the class (MLR8).

Bring the ideas together: follow a top factor down its column and a left factor across its row; the meeting cell gives the product. Explain how a rectangle shows why the table works. Compare the table with an array or an equation: the table has factors and products but no equals signs. Explain a pattern you can use to find another product. Your teacher reviews the completed rectangles, written equations and actual discussions; numerical checks cannot certify these activities.

Finish with a new Edulytics Cool-down: draw a rectangle covering seven rows and four columns in a ten-by-ten table. Identify its product and explain how the rotated rectangle helps check it. This independently written task measures the same area–multiplication connection; it does not reproduce the publisher-gated What’s the Product? assessment.

Optional centers: Capture Squares, stage 6 (multiply with 1–5), and Rectangle Rumble, stage 2 (factors 1–5), reinforce multiplication and area. Five in a Row, stage 7 (add within 1,000 without composing), is supporting practice. Ask which facts were familiar and which strategies helped with unfamiliar products.

KeyConcepts.Title: Factors label sides
KeyConcepts.Definition: The top and left headers show whole-number factors.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Start at the upper-left data square; exclude headers when counting area.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three rows and four columns cover 12 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: A cell is an area product
KeyConcepts.Definition: A table cell is the lower-right corner of a rectangle from the upper-left data square.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply the row factor by the column factor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different rectangles can have the same area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different pairs of factors can have the same product.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check both the product and the table boundaries.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 × 8 and 4 × 6 both give 24 and fit a nine-by-nine table.

KeyConcepts.Title: Patterns connect facts
KeyConcepts.Definition: A new column adds one group of the row factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use familiar products, repeated addition and swapped factors.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 × 5 = 15 and 4 × 5 = 20 differ by one group of 5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Decompose growing arrays
WorkedExamples.Question: How many dots are in the three growing arrangements?
WorkedExamples.Check: Count each dot once; a different valid decomposition must give the same totals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Read a table rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Why does row 3, column 4 contain 12?
Steps: Begin at the upper-left DATA square, excluding the headers.
Trace three rows and four columns.
Write 12 in the lower-right square and connect it to 3 × 4 = 12.
WorkedExamples.Check: The headers label factors but contribute no area squares.

WorkedExamples.Title: More than one 24-square rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Which whole-number rectangles of area 24 fit inside a nine-by-nine table?
WorkedExamples.Method: Find factor pairs and check the table bounds.
Steps: 1 × 24 and 2 × 12 have area 24 but exceed the table.
3 × 8 and 4 × 6 both have product 24 and fit.
Draw from the upper-left data square and label the lower-right product.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every side is between 1 and 9, and every product is 24.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find and explain a pattern
WorkedExamples.Question: How can the products of 5 help with a new fact?
WorkedExamples.Method: Add one equal group and compare swapped factors.
Steps: A rotated four-by-five rectangle shows 5 × 4 = 20 too.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Adjacent products in the row for 5 differ by 5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Write equations and explain the equal groups, rather than only saying the numbers increase.

WorkedExamples.Title: New Edulytics Cool-down
WorkedExamples.Question: A table rectangle covers seven rows and four columns. Find its product and explain.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply its side lengths and rotate to check.
Steps: Read factors 7 and 4 from the headers.
Show both rectangles or an array and explain their equal area.
WorkedExamples.Check: The teacher still reviews the drawing and explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting the header row or column as area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Headers are factor labels outside the data region.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Begin just below and right of the headers and count only data squares.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding 3 and 4 to find a three-by-four rectangle’s area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Side lengths added together do not count the equal square units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply 3 × 4 = 12, or count three rows of four.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying only four by six can make 24.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Three by eight and both rotations also satisfy the task.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every factor pair against the nine-by-nine table.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accepting two by twelve inside the nine-by-nine table.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The product is right but a side extends beyond the table.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check both the area and the stated table boundaries.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Requiring all 100 products to be filled.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks for as many products as students can find, starting with familiar ones.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use known facts and explain patterns; do not turn this exploration into a speed test.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Awarding full activity completion for a correct typed number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Numbers do not establish a rectangle, a pattern explanation or partner participation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Ask the teacher to inspect the drawings, equations and discussion.

SummaryPoints: Table headers are factors; count only data squares.
Start each rectangle at the upper-left data square; its lower-right cell holds the product.
Three by eight and four by six both cover 24 square units and fit the nine-by-nine table.
Use products of 2, 5 and 10 to find other facts; the table need not be completely filled.
Write equations for a pattern and explain with rows, columns or equal groups.
Drawings, notices, questions and partner explanations require teacher review.
